lead: This unit takes discrete-time signals into the frequency domain and then into the z domain. You learn to write a periodic sequence as N harmonics, to describe any sequence by its DTFT, to compute the N-point DFT a computer uses, and to move between a sequence and its Z-transform using the region of convergence. After it you can find h[n] of a difference-equation system, test its stability from a pole-zero plot, and read its frequency response.
about: Chapter 6 moves discrete-time signals into the frequency and z domains. 6.1 gives the discrete-time Fourier series for periodic sequences, where only N harmonics exist. 6.2 lets the period grow to infinity and defines the DTFT, with its property table. 6.3 samples that continuous spectrum at N points to get the DFT, the form every processor uses. 6.4 introduces the Z-transform and the region of convergence, and 6.5 collects the properties that make it a working tool. 6.6 inverts back to x[n], using the ROC to choose the correct side of each pole. 6.7 puts H(z), poles and zeros to work, testing stability and reading the frequency response of a discrete-time LTI system.

chapters.idea: A periodic sequence of period N is a sum of exactly N complex exponentials, and its DTFS coefficients repeat every N.
chapters.depth: Write the analysis equation X[k] = Σ from n = 0 to N-1 of x[n] e^(-j2πkn/N) and the synthesis equation x[n] = (1/N) Σ from k = 0 to N-1 of X[k] e^(j2πkn/N). Define N (period), k (harmonic index) and X[k] (DTFS coefficients). Show why only N distinct frequencies exist: e^(j2π(k+N)n/N) equals e^(j2πkn/N), so X[k] is periodic in k with period N, unlike a continuous-time series. Cover the real-signal symmetry X[N-k] = X*[k], Parseval's relation, and the periodic pulse train. Some syllabi call this the discrete Fourier series (DFS), and some put 1/N on the analysis equation. Do not derive it from the continuous-time series.

figure.title: One period of x[n] and its DTFS magnitudes, N = 8
figure.aria: A row of eight samples of a pulse and the row of the eight DTFS magnitudes, which repeat with period 8.
figure.caption: The two marked magnitudes are equal: X[k] repeats every N, and X[N-k] is the conjugate of X[k].

chapters.example: x[n] is periodic with N = 8 and one period x[0] = x[1] = x[2] = 1, x[3] to x[7] = 0. Using X[k] = Σ from n = 0 to 7 of x[n] e^(-j2πkn/8), find X[0], X[1], X[2], X[3] and check X[7] = X*[1]. Answers: X[0] = 3; X[1] = 2.414 e^(-jπ/4); X[2] = -j; X[3] = 0.293 + j0.293; the check holds.
chapters.trap: Reading k past N-1 and expecting zero: X[8] equals X[0] here. Also the 1/N factor sits on the analysis equation in some books, so state your convention before computing.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 (periodic signals, even and odd signals), Unit 3 (Fourier series of continuous-time signals), Unit 5 (discrete-time signals and sequences).
chapters.leave: The aperiodic case is chapter 6.2; sampling and aliasing belong to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: An aperiodic sequence has a continuous spectrum X(e^(jω)) that repeats every 2π in ω.
chapters.depth: Define X(e^(jω)) = Σ x[n] e^(-jωn) and the inverse x[n] = (1/2π) ∫ over any 2π interval of X(e^(jω)) e^(jωn) dω. State the convergence condition, absolute summability, and that the DTFT is 2π-periodic in ω, so one period ω in (-π, π] holds all the information. Give the pairs: δ[n], a^n u[n], the rectangular pulse, and u[n] with impulses in its spectrum. Cover the properties with one-line proofs: linearity, time shift, frequency shift, time reversal, conjugation and symmetry for real sequences, convolution theorem, multiplication as periodic convolution, Parseval. Show the link to the sampled continuous-time spectrum, X(e^(jωT)) = (1/T) Σ X_c(j(ω - kω_s)), in three lines.

figure.aria: Two curves peaking at ω = 0, the taller one for a = 0.8, and both curving down to a minimum at ω = ±π.
figure.caption: Spectra of x[n] = aⁿu[n] for two values of a; the peak sharpens as a moves towards 1, and each curve repeats every 2π.

chapters.example: For x[n] = (0.8)ⁿu[n], find X(e^(jω)) and evaluate the magnitude at ω = 0, ω = π/2 and ω = π. Answer: X(e^(jω)) = 1/(1 - 0.8e^(-jω)); |X| = 5 at ω = 0, 0.781 at ω = π/2, and 0.556 at ω = π.
chapters.trap: Treating the DTFT as aperiodic in ω and using a single branch like the CTFT. Also u[n] has no ordinary DTFT; it needs impulses at ω = 0, 2π, ...
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 (Fourier transform, convolution and modulation theorems), Unit 5 (sampling), chapter 6.1.
chapters.leave: Numerical evaluation at N frequencies is chapter 6.3; the system use of X(e^(jω)) is chapter 6.7.

chapters.idea: The N-point DFT is the DTFT sampled at N equally spaced frequencies, which makes it a finite matrix calculation.
chapters.depth: Define W_N = e^(-j2π/N), the analysis X[k] = Σ from n = 0 to N-1 of x[n] W_N^(nk), and the synthesis x[n] = (1/N) Σ from k = 0 to N-1 of X[k] W_N^(-nk). Show the matrix form and that X[k] equals X(e^(jω)) at ω = 2πk/N, so the DFT of a length-N sequence is the DTFS of its periodic extension. Cover circular shift, circular convolution and how it differs from linear convolution, zero padding, Parseval for the DFT, and symmetry for real x[n]. Mention that fast algorithms (FFT) compute the same numbers with fewer operations. Applications: spectrum analysers, OFDM in 4G and 5G links, audio frames in a phone.

figure.title: The N-point DFT and back
figure.aria: Four blocks in a row with a return arrow: the signal enters the DFT matrix, produces X[k], and comes back through the inverse DFT.
figure.caption: The whole DFT is one matrix multiplication; the return path is why the inverse needs the factor 1/N.

chapters.example: For N = 4 and x[n] = [1, 2, 3, 4], find X[k] for k = 0 to 3 and check x[0] from the inverse. Answers: X[0] = 10, X[1] = -2 + 2j, X[2] = -2, X[3] = -2 - 2j; and (1/4)(10 - 2 + 2j - 2 - 2 - 2j) = 1 = x[0].
chapters.trap: Using an N-point circular convolution where the linear convolution is wanted. The linear result of two length-N sequences has length 2N-1 and needs zero padding to N ≥ 2N-1.
chapters.leave: Fast algorithms are only mentioned here; the Z-transform view of the DFT is chapter 6.4.

chapters.idea: X(z) is a power series in z⁻¹, and the region of convergence, not the algebra alone, identifies which sequence it came from.
chapters.depth: Define X(z) = Σ x[n] z^(-n) with z a complex number, and convergence as absolute convergence of the sum; the ROC is the set of z where that holds. State the ROC rules: the ROC is a ring, the outside of a circle, or the inside of a circle; it is connected; it contains no poles. Then the cases: finite-length gives the whole z plane except possibly z = 0 or z = ∞; right-sided gives |z| > r₂; left-sided gives |z| < r₁; two-sided gives the annulus r₂ < |z| < r₁. If the unit circle lies in the ROC, the DTFT exists. Give the standard pairs: δ[n] for all z, u[n] for |z| > 1, a^n u[n] for |z| > |a|, -a^n u[-n-1] for |z| < |a|. Draw the pole-zero plot and mention z = e^(sT) as the bridge from the Laplace variable s.

figure.aria: A point at the origin, a pole at radius one third, and the point where the circle of radius one crosses the positive axis.
figure.caption: The ROC for aⁿu[n] with a = 1/3 is everything outside the dashed circle; it contains the unit circle, so the DTFT exists.

chapters.example: Find X(z), the poles and the ROC for x[n] = (1/3)ⁿu[n] - (1/2)ⁿu[-n-1], and say whether the DTFT exists. Answer: X(z) = z/(z - 1/3) + z/(z - 1/2) = z(2z - 5/6)/((z - 1/3)(z - 1/2)), poles at z = 1/3 and z = 1/2, ROC 1/3 < |z| < 1/2; the unit circle is outside the ROC, so no DTFT exists.
chapters.trap: Two different sequences share the same X(z); an answer without the ROC is incomplete. Also a shift can put a pole at z = 0 or z = ∞ and change the edge of the ROC.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4 (Laplace transform and its ROC), chapter 6.2 (the DTFT is X(z) on the unit circle), Unit 1.
chapters.leave: Properties go to chapter 6.5, inversion to 6.6, system analysis to 6.7.

chapters.idea: Every time-domain operation has a simple z-domain counterpart, and the ROC shifts in a predictable way with it.
chapters.depth: State and use: linearity, with ROC at least the intersection; time shift x[n - n₀] ↔ z^(-n₀)X(z), ROC unchanged except possibly at z = 0 or z = ∞; z-domain scaling a^n x[n] ↔ X(z/a) with the ROC scaled by |a|; time reversal x[-n] ↔ X(1/z) with the ROC inverted; multiplication by n, n x[n] ↔ -z dX/dz; convolution x[n]*h[n] ↔ X(z)H(z), ROC at least the intersection; accumulation Σ x[n] ↔ X(z)/(1 - z⁻¹), ROC plus |z| > 1; the initial value theorem x[0] = lim as z → ∞ of X(z) for causal sequences; the final value theorem for causal sequences whose poles are inside the unit circle, plus a pole at z = 1; correlation. Prove each in one line from the definition. Say clearly that ROC statements are at least the intersection, because pole-zero cancellation can enlarge the ROC.

figure.aria: A root box for Z-transform properties with five child boxes, each holding one time-domain operation and its z-domain effect.
figure.caption: One root, five working rules: each child turns a time-domain operation into arithmetic on X(z).

chapters.example: x[n] = (0.5)ⁿu[n] has X(z) = z/(z - 0.5) with ROC |z| > 0.5. Use the multiplication-by-n property to find the Z-transform of y[n] = n(0.5)ⁿu[n] and state its ROC. Answer: -z dX/dz = 0.5z/(z - 0.5)², ROC |z| > 0.5.
chapters.trap: Quoting the ROC as exactly the intersection of two ROCs when a pole has cancelled. And never use the initial value theorem on a sequence that is not causal.
chapters.leave: Inversion methods are chapter 6.6; applying H(z) to a system is chapter 6.7.

chapters.idea: To recover x[n] you invert the algebra and then let the ROC decide which side of each pole the sequence lies on.
chapters.depth: Quote the contour integral x[n] = (1/2πj) ∮ X(z) z^(n-1) dz and say we evaluate it by three practical methods. (i) Power series or long division: expand in powers of z⁻¹ when the ROC is |z| > r (right-sided) and in powers of z when it is |z| < r (left-sided), then read x[n] off the coefficients. (ii) Partial fractions: form X(z)/z, split into first-order terms, convert each with the table, and pick aⁿu[n] or -aⁿu[-n-1] from the ROC. (iii) Residues: sum the residues of X(z) z^(n-1) at the poles inside the ROC, with care at z = 0 and at repeated poles. Include repeated and complex poles. Some syllabi call this inversion of the Z-transform.

figure.title: Partial fractions with the ROC deciding the side
figure.aria: A downward flow from X(z) through partial fractions to one pole, which splits into two branches that end at the same output x[n].
figure.caption: One pole gives two different sequences; only the ROC chooses which branch the answer takes.

chapters.example: Find x[n] for X(z) = 1/((1 - 0.5z⁻¹)(1 - 2z⁻¹)) with ROC 0.5 < |z| < 2. Answer: A = -1/3 for the pole at 0.5, B = 4/3 for the pole at 2; the inner pole is right-sided and the outer pole is left-sided, so x[n] = -(1/3)(0.5)ⁿu[n] - (4/3)(2)ⁿu[-n-1].
chapters.trap: Choosing u[n] for every term out of habit. The same partial fraction gives a causal or an anti-causal term depending only on the ROC.
chapters.leave: The system response from H(z) is chapter 6.7.

chapters.idea: H(z) = Y(z)/X(z) turns a difference equation into algebra, and its poles together with the unit circle settle stability and frequency response.
chapters.depth: Define H(z) = Y(z)/X(z) for zero initial conditions and derive H(z) = (Σ b_k z^(-k))/(Σ a_k z^(-k)) from Σ a_k y[n-k] = Σ b_k x[n-k]. State that h[n] is the inverse transform of H(z). Causality: the ROC is the outside of a circle including z = ∞. BIBO stability: the ROC contains the unit circle; for a causal system that means every pole lies strictly inside |z| = 1. Frequency response H(e^(jω)) = H(z) at z = e^(jω), meaningful when the ROC contains the unit circle; sketch magnitude and phase. Solve a difference equation with initial conditions using the one-sided Z-transform and split the zero-input and zero-state parts; give the steady-state response to a sinusoid from |H| and the angle of H at that ω. Inverse systems: H_i(z) = 1/H(z) has the zeros of H as poles, and only a few syllabi list deconvolution.

figure.aria: Two low-pass curves, the one for a pole at 0.9 rising to a peak of ten at ω = 0, the one for 0.5 peaking at two.
figure.caption: Magnitude response of 1/(1 - a z⁻¹): the closer the pole to the unit circle, the higher and sharper the peak at ω = 0.

chapters.example: A system obeys y[n] - 0.5y[n-1] = x[n] with zero initial conditions. Find H(z) and its ROC, decide causality and stability, give h[n], and find the step response for x[n] = u[n]. Answer: H(z) = 1/(1 - 0.5z⁻¹), pole at 0.5, ROC |z| > 0.5, so the system is causal and stable; h[n] = (0.5)ⁿu[n]; y[n] = (2 - (0.5)ⁿ)u[n].
chapters.trap: Reading stability from pole positions alone. Stability is a statement about the ROC; a causal system is stable only when the ROC, which is outside the largest pole, still covers the unit circle. Also 1/H(z) can be unstable while H(z) is stable.
chapters.prereq: chapters 6.4 to 6.6, Unit 5 (difference equations), Unit 2 (BIBO stability and causality).
chapters.leave: DTFT properties are chapter 6.2; sampling and reconstruction are Unit 5.
